title: The maths you need

15.3 Vectors, matrices and the dot product
15.5 Statistics you will use every week

html:
Purpose. You do not need to be a mathematician to be a good machine learning engineer. You need to understand what each formula is trying to do. This chapter collects the maths used in the book, each piece with its purpose and a worked example, and tells you what to study first.

Key ideas

  • A formula is a goal written for a computer. Ask what it is for, and say it in words.
  • Order of importance (Infinite Codes): statistics and probability, then linear algebra, then a few ideas from calculus, then the machine learning concepts themselves.
  • You need four tools: vectors and dot products, derivatives and the chain rule, basic statistics, and Bayes' theorem.

15.1 Think in purposes

Infinite Codes' advice is to stop memorizing equations and ask what each is trying to do, then write it in plain language. Students who memorize the algorithms and call scikit-learn get great accuracy in their project and nonsense on real data, because they cannot say why a model suits one problem and not another. The video's example is the linear regression loss: "I want the line to be close to the points" becomes distance equals prediction minus truth, squared so it is positive, added over all points, which is the residual sum of squares (Chapters 4 and 5). Mathematical formulas just help us tell the computer our goals. Every formula in this book has its one-sentence purpose beside it.

15.2 The checklist, and where each item appears here

Area Ideas Where in this book
Statistics and probability mean, median, variance, covariance, correlation; distributions, the normal distribution, the central limit theorem; standard deviation and z-scores; significance and hypothesis tests; the multiple comparisons problem; conditional probability, Bayes Chapters 3, 8, 12, 15
Linear algebra vectors, matrices, dot product, norms, transpose, inverse, rank Chapters 7, 8, 11, 18
Calculus derivatives, the chain rule Chapters 6, 10, 14
Machine learning concepts loss functions, gradient descent, regularization, train, validation and test sets, cross-validation, overfitting, bias and variance, data quality, model selection Chapters 3 to 12

15.3 Vectors, matrices and the dot product

A vector is a list of numbers: the features of one loan, the weights of a model. A matrix is a table of numbers: all the loans, one per row. Three operations cover most of what you need:

  • Dot product: multiply matching entries and add. [2, 3] . [10, 4] = 32. The prediction of every linear model is one (Chapter 7).
  • Matrix times vector: a dot product of every row with the vector. X @ w predicts for all m rows at once.
  • Norm: the length of a vector, the square root of the sum of its squares. The squared norm of the weights is the L2 penalty of Chapter 11.

Cosine similarity compares the direction of two vectors: the dot product divided by the product of their lengths. It is 1 for the same direction, 0 for unrelated, and -1 for opposite. It is how embeddings are compared in Chapter 18.

15.4 Derivatives and the chain rule

The derivative of a function is its slope at a point: how much the output changes per tiny change of the input. For a function of several inputs, the partial derivative is the slope along one of them, and the gradient is the vector of all the partial derivatives. Gradient descent (Chapter 6) simply walks against the gradient.

The chain rule handles a function inside a function: multiply the slope of the outer function by the slope of the inner one. The squared error of one example is (w x - y) squared. The inner function is w x - y, with slope x with respect to w. The outer function is its square, with slope 2 (w x - y). So the derivative with respect to w is 2 (w x - y) x. This is where the 2 that cancels the 1/2 of the cost comes from (Chapter 5). Backpropagation (Chapter 14) is this same rule applied layer after layer.

import numpy as np

a, b = np.array([1, 0]), np.array([1, 1])
cos = a @ b / (np.linalg.norm(a) * np.linalg.norm(b))
print(round(cos, 3))                # 0.707  (the angle between them is 45 degrees)

f = lambda w: (w * 3 - 5) ** 2     # squared error of one example: x = 3, y = 5
print(2 * (2 * 3 - 5) * 3)         # 6    the slope at w = 2, from the chain rule
print(round((f(2 + 1e-6) - f(2 - 1e-6)) / 2e-6, 3))   # 6.0  the slope measured numerically

The last two lines are a useful habit: when you derive a gradient by hand, check it against a numerical slope.

15.5 Statistics you will use every week

  • Mean and median: the average, and the middle value. The median is not moved by outliers.
  • Variance and standard deviation: how spread out the values are. The standard deviation is the square root of the variance, in the original units. A z-score says how many standard deviations a value is from the mean (Chapter 8): a loan of 1,000 when the mean is 600 and the standard deviation is 450 has a z-score of 0.89.
  • Correlation: from -1 to 1, how closely two columns move together in a straight-line way. It never proves cause.
  • The normal distribution: the bell curve. About 68% of values lie within 1 standard deviation of the mean, 95% within 2, and 99.7% within 3.
  • The central limit theorem: the averages of many random samples are roughly bell-shaped, whatever the shape of the original data. It is why so many statistical tests work.
  • Samples and populations: you almost never see the whole population, only a sample. The law of large numbers says that sample averages settle on the truth as the sample grows.
  • Significance and the p-value: a hypothesis test asks "if there were no real effect, how surprising would data like this be?" A small p-value (often under 0.05) means very surprising. It does not give the probability that the effect is real.
  • The multiple comparisons problem: test 20 unrelated things at the 5% level, and the chance that at least one looks "significant" by luck is 1 - 0.95^20, about 64%. Fixes, such as the Bonferroni correction, demand a stricter threshold, the 5% divided by the number of tests. In machine learning the same trap appears when you try dozens of models and features and report the best one: keep a test set that you use once.

15.6 Probability and Bayes' theorem

The probability of A given B, written P(A | B), is the chance of A when you know B has happened. Bayes' theorem turns it around:

P(A∣B)=P(B∣A) P(A)P(B)P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(B \mid A)\, P(A)}{P(B)}

It shows why precision (Chapter 12) is so often a disappointment. Using the loan example of Chapter 12: 5% of loans default, the model flags 70% of the defaulters, and it wrongly flags 2.6% of the good loans (25 of 950). If a loan is flagged, what is the chance it really defaults?

  • P(flag and default) = 0.7 x 0.05 = 0.035.
  • P(flag and good loan) = 0.026 x 0.95 = 0.025.
  • P(default | flag) = 0.035 / (0.035 + 0.025) = 0.583.

The answer, 58%, is exactly the precision from the confusion matrix. Because defaults are rare, even a model with a 2.6% false alarm rate produces false alarms that are nearly as numerous as real hits. Naive Bayes (Chapter 13) is this theorem applied to every feature, with the independence assumption.

15.7 What to study first

Start with statistics, because it makes you better at picking and judging models. Then linear algebra if you want neural networks, then enough calculus for derivatives and the chain rule. Free resources named in the video: Khan Academy for statistics, linear algebra and calculus (start here), the free book An Introduction to Statistical Learning and its video series, and 3Blue1Brown for visual explanations.

Loan example. The probability that a flagged loan really defaults (58%) is a conditional probability, computed with Bayes. The weight penalty is a norm. The cost is a sum of squares, its slopes come from the chain rule, and its minimum is found with gradient descent. Nothing in the loan project needs more maths than this chapter.

Common mistakes

  • Memorizing a formula without being able to say what it is for.
  • Reading correlation as cause, or a small p-value as "the effect is real".
  • Trying many things and reporting only the best one without a fresh test.
  • Confusing P(A | B) with P(B | A): the chance of a flag given a default (70%) is not the chance of a default given a flag (58%).

Check yourself

  • Compute the cosine similarity of [1, 0] and [0, 1], and of [2, 2] and [1, 1].
  • Derive the derivative of (w x - y) squared with respect to w.
  • You run 40 tests at the 5% level on random data. About how many will look significant by chance?
  • A disease affects 1% of people. A test finds 90% of the sick and wrongly flags 9% of the healthy. If you test positive, what is the chance you are sick?
Show answers

(1) 0, and 1. (2) 2 (w x - y) x, by the chain rule. (3) About 2 (40 x 0.05). (4) 0.9 x 0.01 = 0.009 of the sick flagged; 0.09 x 0.99 = 0.0891 of the healthy flagged; 0.009 / (0.009 + 0.0891) = about 9%. Most positives are false alarms because the disease is rare.
